title: How Music Steers You
objective: After this level you can spot how a score cues emotions, and test it by imagining a scene with different music or silence.
summary: In Boltz's study, positive or negative music changed how viewers read ambiguous clips and what they remembered. Test a score by imagining silence.

cards.headline: Would you trust this character if the music changed?
cards.body: A man walks up to a house at dusk. Is he coming home, or coming to do harm? The pictures won't say. Researchers found that the music will, and that you may not notice it deciding for you.

cards.headline: The experiment
cards.body: Psychologist Marilyn Boltz tested it in a 2001 study. Viewers watched three ambiguous film clips. Some heard positive music, some negative music, and some heard none. Then they predicted how each film would end and judged what the main characters were like and what they wanted. The pictures were identical for everyone. Only the soundtrack changed.

cards.headline: Same pictures, different story
cards.body: Compared with viewers who heard no music, the music groups read the clips in the music's mood, and later remembered them that way too. Boltz concluded that music supplies a framework for reading characters and motives, and guides attention, shaping which details viewers remember or misremember.

cards.headline: Test it: switch the music off
cards.body: You can run Boltz's control group in your head. Picture the scene in silence, then with the opposite music. Whatever changes was the score's work, not the picture's. Remember Level 38: most film music is non-diegetic. The characters can't hear it. It's a message addressed to you, so it's worth asking what it's telling you to feel.

cards.headline: How Music Steers You: done
learned: Boltz: same clips, different music, different stories
Music biases what you infer and remember
Test a score by imagining silence
Non-diegetic music speaks only to you

questions.prompt: In Boltz's 2001 study, what did the three groups of viewers have that differed?

options.label: Different film clips
options.rationale: Everyone saw the same ambiguous clips.

options.label: Different actors in the scenes
options.rationale: The pictures were identical for everyone.

options.label: Positive music, negative music, or no music

questions.explanation: Only the soundtrack varied: positive music, negative music or none.

questions.prompt: A chase scene is scored with bouncy, cheerful music. Based on Boltz's findings, how will most viewers likely read it?

options.label: As lighter and less threatening, in the music's mood
Exactly as they would in silence
options.rationale: Music biased readings compared with no music.

options.label: As more frightening, because music always adds tension
options.rationale: The bias follows the music's mood.

options.label: They won't remember any of it
options.rationale: Music shaped memory; it didn't erase it.

questions.explanation: Music biased viewers' interpretations toward its own mood, so cheerful music pulls a chase toward comedy.

questions.prompt: Level 38 says most film scores are non-diegetic. What does that mean for how a score steers you?

options.label: The characters hear it and react, so you copy them
options.rationale: Non-diegetic music is heard only by the audience.

options.label: It is addressed to you alone, since the characters can't hear it
It must come from a radio in the scene
It is recorded live on set with the dialogue
options.rationale: Most scores come from outside the story world.

questions.explanation: Non-diegetic music comes from outside the story world: you hear it, the characters don't, so its message is for you.
